## 🎯 Learning Objectives

::: {style="font-size: 34px"}
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:

- **Distinguish** observable, model-free volatility measures from model-based ones, and **show** that RiskMetrics is an IGARCH
- **Explain** why realized volatility converges to integrated volatility, and what microstructure noise does to it
- **Write** a multiplicative error model and the ACD model for durations
- **Model** the direction of change (autologit) and conditional quantiles (VaR, CAViaR)
- **Backtest** a VaR forecast with Kupiec's test on real data
:::

## 🔁 Warm-up from last time {.quiz-question}

You search over the middle 70% of the sample for one break in a mean and find $\sup W = 7.9$. At 5%, what do you conclude?

- [No evidence of a break: 7.9 is below Andrews' critical value 8.68]{.correct data-explanation="✅ The date was searched for, so sup W must be compared with the critical value of sup Q(r) over [0.15, 0.85], which is 8.68 for one coefficient, not with the χ²₁ value 3.84."}
- A break: 7.9 exceeds the $\chi^2_1$ critical value 3.84
- A break, since the CUSUM test is never needed after sup-W
- Nothing can be said until the number of breaks is fixed

## 🗺️ Where We Are

::: {style="font-size: 32px"}
Lecture 15 modelled the conditional variance $\sigma_t^2$ with GARCH. Lecture 16 asked whether such parameters are stable.

$\sigma_t^2$ is never observed: it exists only inside a model, and is only as good as the model's mean and variance equations.

::: {.fragment}
This last lecture asks three questions.

- Can volatility be **measured** rather than modelled?
- How do we model other positive quantities, such as the time between trades?
- How do we forecast what risk managers actually report: a **quantile** of tomorrow's return?
:::
:::

---

## ❓ The Question

::: {.callout-important}
## The number the regulator sees
Every day a bank reports its 1-day 99% Value-at-Risk: a loss it expects to exceed on only 1 day in 100. Every quarter the regulator counts the days on which the loss was larger.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
Too many such days and the bank holds more capital. To get the count right the bank needs a good volatility measure, a good model of the tails, and a way to **test** its own quantile forecasts.
:::

---

## 📐 Measures of Daily Volatility

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
**Observable, model-free:**

- $|r_t|$ and $r_t^2$: the earliest measures. $E_{t-1}r_t^2 = \sigma_t^2$ when $\mu_t = 0$, but a single squared return is very noisy
- JPMorgan's **RiskMetrics**, an exponentially weighted average of past squared returns:
$$RM_t = (1 - 0.94)\sum_{i=0}^{\infty} 0.94^{\,i}\, r_{t-i}^2$$

**Not observable, model-based:**

- $\hat\sigma_t^2$ from an ARCH-type model. It is only as good as the model's conditional mean and variance equations
:::

---

## 📐 RiskMetrics Is an IGARCH

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
Split off the first term of the sum. With $\lambda = 0.94$,
$$\sigma_{t+1 \mid t}^2 = (1-\lambda)\sum_{i \ge 0}\lambda^i r_{t-i}^2 = (1-\lambda)\, r_t^2 + \lambda\,\sigma_{t \mid t-1}^2 .$$

This is GARCH(1,1) without a constant:
$$\omega = 0, \qquad \alpha = 1 - \lambda = 0.06, \qquad \beta = \lambda = 0.94, \qquad \alpha + \beta = 1 .$$

- Integrated GARCH: shocks to the variance never die out, and there is no long-run level to revert to
- Nothing is estimated: $\lambda = 0.94$ is fixed for all daily series
- Weights halve every $\ln 0.5 / \ln 0.94 = 11.2$ days
:::

---

## 📐 Realized Volatility

::: {style="font-size: 29px"}
The daily return $r_t = \log p_{\text{close}} - \log p_{\text{open}}$ sees only two prices. Very different intraday paths give the same $r_t$.

Split day $t$ into $m$ intervals with intraday returns $r_{t,i}$, $i = 1, \dots, m$, and define
$$RV_t = \sum_{i=1}^m r_{t,i}^2 \qquad \text{(Andersen, Bollerslev, Diebold and co-authors, 2000s).}$$

Like $|r_t|$ and $r_t^2$, it is **observable** and **model-free**. Unlike them, it is far less noisy, as the next two slides show.
:::

---

## 📈 Same Return, Different Days

```{r}
#| label: two-paths
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 3.8
set.seed(2026)
m <- 390; s <- (0:m) / m
bridge <- function(sd) { b <- c(0, cumsum(rnorm(m, 0, sd / sqrt(m)))); b - s * b[m + 1] }
calm  <- 0.5 * s + bridge(0.4)                         # log price in %, close - open = 0.5
storm <- 0.5 * s + bridge(2.0)
rv <- function(x) sum(diff(x)^2)
df <- rbind(data.frame(s = s, p = calm,  day = sprintf("calm day:  RV = %.2f", rv(calm))),
            data.frame(s = s, p = storm, day = sprintf("stormy day: RV = %.2f", rv(storm))))
ggplot(df, aes(s, p, colour = day)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#8ba3c7", "#8b2635"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "time of day (open = 0, close = 1)", y = "log price − log open (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Both days open at 0 and close at $+0.5\%$, so $r_t = 0.5$ and $r_t^2 = 0.25$ on each. The one-minute returns tell them apart: realized variance differs by a factor of about 25.
:::

---

## 📐 Why Realized Volatility Works

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
Suppose the log price within the day follows
$$d\log p_{t+s} = \mu_{t+s}\,ds + \sigma_{t+s}\,dW_{t+s}, \qquad s \in [0, 1],$$
with $\sigma^2_{t+s}$ the **instantaneous volatility**. Then as $m \to \infty$
$$RV_t \xrightarrow{p} IV_t = \int_0^1 \sigma_{t+s}^2\,ds \qquad \text{(integrated volatility)},$$
with a mixed-normal CLT at rate $\sqrt m$.

- The drift $\mu_{t+s}$ contributes only $O(m^{-1})$ and can be neglected
- A GARCH, by contrast, must get the conditional mean right before its $\hat\sigma_t^2$ means anything
:::

---

## 📐 Covariance, Noise, and the Choice of $m$

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
**Multivariate analogue.** For a vector of intraday returns, the realized covariance matrix
$$RC_t = \sum_{i=1}^m r_{t,i}\, r_{t,i}' .$$

**But $m$ is finite**, and one would like it large. At very high frequencies prices bounce between bid and ask, and ticks are discrete. This **market microstructure noise** adds a term to every $r_{t,i}^2$, and the bias grows with $m$.

In practice the sampling interval is about **5 to 15 minutes**: fine enough for $RV_t$ to be precise, coarse enough for the noise to be small.
:::

---

## 💻 Noise and the Sampling Frequency

```{r}
#| label: signature
#| code-summary: "📦 200 simulated days, second by second"
set.seed(2026)
n_sec <- 23400; days <- 200; s <- (1:n_sec) / n_sec
sig <- 0.01 * sqrt(0.6 + 3.2 * (s - 0.5)^2)                    # U-shaped intraday vol
IV <- mean(sig^2)                                              # integrated variance per day
grid <- c(13, 26, 78, 390, 1170, 4680, 23400)                  # 30 min ... 1 second
res <- replicate(days, {
  lp <- cumsum(sig * rnorm(n_sec) / sqrt(n_sec))               # efficient log price
  obs <- lp + rnorm(n_sec, 0, 0.0001)                          # + noise, 1 basis point
  sapply(grid, function(m) { k <- seq(n_sec / m, n_sec, by = n_sec / m)
    c(clean = sum(diff(c(0, lp[k]))^2), noisy = sum(diff(c(0, obs[k]))^2)) })
})
round(cbind(m = grid, clean = rowMeans(res[1, , ]) / IV, noisy = rowMeans(res[2, , ]) / IV), 2)
```

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Average $RV_t / IV_t$ over 200 simulated days. Without noise it is 1 at every $m$. With a one-basis-point noise, it is fine at 5 minutes ($m = 78$) and more than six times too large at one second.
:::

---

## 📐 Multiplicative Error Models

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
Many quantities in finance are **positive**: $RV_t$, the daily range, $|r_t|$, and the **durations** $d_t = t_i - t_{i-1}$ between transactions. Durations cluster: busy periods have short gaps.

::: {.callout-note}
## MEM (Engle, 2002)
$$x_t = \psi_t\,\varepsilon_t, \qquad \psi_t = E_{t-1}x_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \text{iid } \mathcal D(1),\ \ \varepsilon_t > 0,\ E\varepsilon_t = 1 .$$
:::

It is the positive analogue of $r_t = \sigma_t\eta_t$, $\eta_t \sim (0, 1)$: there the shock scales a **standard deviation**, here it scales a **mean**.
:::

---

## 📐 The ACD Model

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
For durations, Engle & Russell (1998): **A**utoregressive **C**onditional **D**uration,
$$d_t = \psi_t\varepsilon_t, \qquad \text{ACD}(1,1):\ \ \psi_t = \omega + \alpha\, d_{t-1} + \beta\,\psi_{t-1}, \qquad \omega > 0,\ \alpha, \beta \ge 0,$$
with $\alpha + \beta < 1$ for a finite unconditional mean duration $\omega/(1-\alpha-\beta)$.

| Choice of $\mathcal D$ | Method | Analogue in GARCH |
|---|---|---|
| Standard exponential | QMLE, $\ell_t = -\log\psi_t - d_t/\psi_t$ | Gaussian QMLE |
| Weibull$(\lambda)$, Burr$(\lambda, \mu)$ | MLE | Student-$t$ MLE |

The exponential QMLE is consistent whenever $\psi_t$ is correctly specified, whatever the true $\mathcal D$.
:::

---

## 📐 Beyond Mean and Variance

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
So far dynamic models have targeted

- ✓ the conditional **mean** (ARMA, VAR, TAR)
- ✓ the conditional **variance** (GARCH, SV, RV)
- ✓ the conditional **density**: conditional skewness and kurtosis (ARCD)

::: {.fragment}
Two more objects are often what a user actually needs:

- the **direction** of tomorrow's move, $\mathbb 1\{r_t > 0\}$
- a **quantile** of tomorrow's return: Value-at-Risk
:::
:::

---

## 📐 Direction of Change: Autologit

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
The sign indicator has conditional mean equal to a conditional probability:
$$E_{t-1}\,\mathbb 1\{r_t > 0\} = \Pr_{t-1}\{r_t > 0\}.$$

**Autologit(1,1):**
$$\Pr_{t-1}\{r_t > 0\} = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\{-w_t\}}, \qquad w_t = \varphi + \alpha\,\mathbb 1\{r_{t-1} > 0\} + \gamma\, r_{t-1} + \beta\, w_{t-1} .$$

- $w_t$ plays the role of $\sigma_t^2$ in GARCH: a recursion driven by yesterday's data and its own lag
- Estimated by maximum likelihood with the Bernoulli likelihood $\sum_t \big[\mathbb 1\{r_t>0\}\log P_t + \mathbb 1\{r_t \le 0\}\log(1 - P_t)\big]$
:::

---

## 📐 Conditional Quantiles: Value-at-Risk

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
::: {.callout-note}
## Value-at-Risk
The $(1-p)\cdot 100\%$ VaR is the conditional $p$-quantile of the return:
$$\Pr_{t-1}\big\{r_t \le \mathrm{VaR}_t\big\} = p .$$
:::

**Indirect modelling.** If $(r_t - \mu_t)/\sigma_t = \eta_t \sim \text{iid } \mathcal D(0, 1, \vartheta)$, estimate $\hat\mu_t$, $\hat\sigma_t$ and the density $\hat f_{\mathcal D}$, then
$$\widehat{\mathrm{VaR}}_t = \hat\mu_t + \hat\sigma_t\, q_p\big(\hat f_{\mathcal D}\big),$$
with $q_p$ the $p$-quantile of the fitted standardised distribution. Normal: $q_{0.01} = -2.326$, $q_{0.05} = -1.645$.
:::

---

## 📐 Direct Modelling: CAViaR

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
Model the quantile itself, with no distribution (Engle & Manganelli, 2004):
$$r_t = q_t^p + e_t, \qquad \text{Quantile}_p\big(e_t \mid I_{t-1}\big) = 0,$$
$$q_t^p = \omega + \beta\, q_{t-1}^p + \alpha\, g(r_{t-1}), \qquad \text{e.g. } g(r) = |r| .$$

Estimate by **quantile regression**: minimise
$$\sum_t \rho_p\big(r_t - q_t^p\big), \qquad \rho_p(u) = u\,\big(p - \mathbb 1\{u < 0\}\big).$$

The check function $\rho_p$ penalises a return below the quantile with weight $1-p$ and one above it with weight $p$; its minimiser is the $p$-quantile.
:::

---

## 🧪 Backtesting a VaR

::: {style="font-size: 29px"}
Define the **hit** $I_t = \mathbb 1\{r_t < \widehat{\mathrm{VaR}}_t\}$. If the VaR is correct, the hits are iid Bernoulli($p$). With $x$ hits in $n$ days and $\hat\pi = x/n$, Kupiec's unconditional-coverage test is
$$LR_{uc} = -2\log\big[(1-p)^{n-x}p^{x}\big] + 2\log\big[(1-\hat\pi)^{n-x}\hat\pi^{x}\big] \xrightarrow[H_0]{d} \chi^2_1 .$$

- Reject at 5% if $LR_{uc} > 3.84$: too many hits **or** too few
- Christoffersen (1998) adds a test that the hits are **independent**: clustered hits mean the VaR reacts too slowly

[Not in the 2016 notes: added from Kupiec (1995) and Christoffersen (1998).]{.gapnote}
:::

---

## ✏️ Worked Example: RiskMetrics VaR

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Yesterday $\sigma_{t \mid t-1}^2 = 1.20$ ($\%^2$) and the index fell $r_t = -2.5\%$. A fund holds 10 million USD.

::: {.fragment}
**1. Update.** $\sigma_{t+1 \mid t}^2 = 0.06 \times 6.25 + 0.94 \times 1.20 = 0.375 + 1.128 = 1.503$, so $\sigma_{t+1 \mid t} = 1.226\%$.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**2. VaR at 99%.** $\mathrm{VaR}_{t+1} = -2.326 \times 1.226 = -2.85\%$: a loss above 285,000 USD on 1 day in 100.
:::

:::

---

## ✏️ Worked Example: Backtesting It

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Over $n = 1000$ days the same VaR is exceeded $x = 18$ times, against $10$ expected. So $\hat\pi = 0.018$ and

::: {.fragment}
$$\begin{aligned} LR_{uc} &= -2\,[982 \ln 0.99 + 18 \ln 0.01] + 2\,[982 \ln 0.982 + 18 \ln 0.018] \\ &= 185.53 - 180.30 = 5.23 > 3.84 . \end{aligned}$$
Reject: the VaR is exceeded too often. With 6 hits instead, $LR_{uc} = 1.89$: fewer hits than expected, but not significantly so.
:::
:::

## 🧠 Think-Pair-Share

```{r}
#| label: tps-timer
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(minutes = 3, seconds = 0, top = 0, right = 0,
                     font_size = "2em", warn_when = 30)
```

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
1. A colleague writes RiskMetrics as $\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha r_{t-1}^2 + \beta\sigma_{t-1}^2$ with $\alpha = 0.94$. What should $\omega$, $\alpha$, $\beta$ be? Is the model covariance stationary?

2. A bank's 99% VaR was exceeded on 4 of the last 250 days. Does Kupiec's test reject?

3. Why is it hopeless to backtest a 99% VaR on one month of data?
:::

---

## ✅ Think-Pair-Share: Solution

::: {style="font-size: 29px"}
1. $\omega = 0$, $\alpha = 1 - \lambda = 0.06$, $\beta = \lambda = 0.94$. Since $\alpha + \beta = 1$ it is an IGARCH: **not** covariance stationary, and there is no unconditional variance.

2. $\hat\pi = 0.016$ and
$$\begin{aligned} LR_{uc} &= -2[246\ln 0.99 + 4\ln 0.01] + 2[246\ln 0.984 + 4\ln 0.016] \\ &= 41.79 - 41.02 = 0.77 < 3.84 . \end{aligned}$$
No rejection: 4 hits against 2.5 expected is within sampling error.

3. In 21 days the expected number of hits is $0.21$. Zero hits has probability 0.81 if the VaR is right, and remains likely if it is badly wrong, so the test has almost no power.
:::

## 🎛️ Explore: The RiskMetrics Decay $\lambda$

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof lam = {
  const input = Inputs.range([0.80, 0.995], {value: 0.94, step: 0.005, label: "λ (decay)"});
  ['pointerdown','touchstart','mousedown','click','wheel','pointermove','touchmove']
    .forEach(e => input.addEventListener(e, ev => ev.stopPropagation()));
  return input;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ewma = {
  const r = ret, n = r.length, out = [];
  let s2 = r.slice(0, 60).reduce((a, b) => a + b * b, 0) / 60, hits = 0, cnt = 0;
  for (let t = 1; t < n; t++) {
    s2 = lam * s2 + (1 - lam) * r[t - 1] ** 2;
    const v = -2.326 * Math.sqrt(s2);
    const hit = t >= 250 && r[t] < v;
    if (t >= 250) { cnt++; if (hit) hits++; }
    out.push({t, r: r[t], v, hit});
  }
  const p = 0.01, ph = hits / cnt;
  const LR = -2 * ((cnt - hits) * Math.log(1 - p) + hits * Math.log(p))
             + 2 * ((cnt - hits) * Math.log(1 - ph) + hits * Math.log(ph));
  return {out, hits, cnt, LR};
}
```

  style: {fontSize: "18px"},

  marks: [

    Plot.lineY(ewma.out, {x: "t", y: "v", stroke: "#2f4b7c", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot(ewma.out.filter(d => d.hit), {x: "t", y: "r", r: 4, fill: "#8b2635"})

## 💰 Case Study: Backtesting S&P 500 VaR

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-note}
## 📈 The question

Three ways to forecast tomorrow's 1% and 5% quantile of the S&P 500 return.

1. Does RiskMetrics with normal quantiles pass Kupiec's test?
2. Does model-free historical simulation do better?
3. Does replacing the normal quantile by the empirical one (indirect modelling with $\hat f_{\mathcal D}$) fix the tails?
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-tip}
## 📊 The data

**Series**: S&P 500 close, FRED `SP500`

**Period**: Oct 2016 – Oct 2026; VaR evaluated on the last 2,261 days

**Transformation**: $r_t = 100\,\Delta\log P_t$; $\mu_t = 0$; first 250 days used only to start the forecasts
:::
:::
::::

```{.r .display-only}
sp <- read.csv("https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=SP500")
```

---

## 💰 Case Study: Hit Rates and Kupiec

```{r}
#| label: case-var
#| code-summary: "📦 RiskMetrics, historical simulation, filtered HS; Kupiec LR"
r <- r_all; n <- length(r); ev <- 251:n
s2 <- numeric(n); s2[1] <- mean(r[1:60]^2)
for (t in 2:n) s2[t] <- 0.94 * s2[t - 1] + 0.06 * r[t - 1]^2      # sigma^2_{t|t-1}
z <- r / sqrt(s2)                                                  # standardised returns
kupiec <- function(hit, p) { x <- sum(hit); m <- length(hit); ph <- x / m
  LR <- -2 * ((m - x) * log(1 - p) + x * log(p)) + 2 * ((m - x) * log(1 - ph) + x * log(ph))
  c(hit_rate = 100 * ph, LR = LR, p_value = pchisq(LR, 1, lower.tail = FALSE)) }
var_fc <- function(p) list(
  RiskMetrics_normal = qnorm(p) * sqrt(s2[ev]),
  historical_250d    = sapply(ev, function(t) quantile(r[(t - 250):(t - 1)], p)),
  filtered_HS        = sapply(ev, function(t) sqrt(s2[t]) * quantile(z[1:(t - 1)], p)))
V1 <- var_fc(0.01); V5 <- var_fc(0.05)
round(rbind(t(sapply(V1, function(v) kupiec(r[ev] < v, 0.01))),
            t(sapply(V5, function(v) kupiec(r[ev] < v, 0.05)))), 3) |>
  `rownames<-`(paste(rep(c("1%:", "5%:"), each = 3), names(V1)))
```

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Hit rates in %, against 1 and 5. Read the 1% rows first.
:::

## 💰 Case Study: The Normal Tail Fails

```{r}
#| label: case-fig
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.9
dd <- d_all[ev]; v <- V1$RiskMetrics_normal; vf <- V1$filtered_HS
lab_n <- "99% VaR, RiskMetrics normal"; lab_f <- "99% VaR, filtered HS"
lines <- rbind(data.frame(d = dd, v = v, what = lab_n), data.frame(d = dd, v = vf, what = lab_f))
hits <- data.frame(d = dd, r = r[ev])[r[ev] < v, ]
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(d = dd, r = r[ev]), aes(d, r), colour = "#d5dde9", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = lines, aes(d, v, colour = what), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = hits, aes(d, r), colour = "#8b2635", size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(c("#2f4b7c", "#e08a2c"), c(lab_n, lab_f)), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-8, 6)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Daily return (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
**What the data say:** at 5% all three forecasts pass. At 1% the normal RiskMetrics VaR is exceeded on 2.3% of days (red dots), and Kupiec rejects decisively; historical simulation, which reacts slowly, is also rejected. Keeping RiskMetrics for $\sigma_t$ but taking the quantile from the standardised returns passes. The failure is the normal tail, not the volatility model.
:::

---

## 📈 VIX: Volatility Looking Forward

```{r}
#| label: vix
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.5
vix <- read.csv("data/vix.csv"); vix$VIXCLS <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(vix$VIXCLS))
mm <- merge(data.frame(date = d_all, r = r_all, rm = sqrt(252 * s2)),
            data.frame(date = as.Date(vix$observation_date), vix = vix$VIXCLS))
mm <- na.omit(mm); N <- nrow(mm)
mm$rv_fwd <- c(sapply(1:(N - 21), function(i) sqrt(252 / 21 * sum(mm$r[(i + 1):(i + 21)]^2))),
               rep(NA, 21))                                    # next 21 days, annualised
ok <- !is.na(mm$rv_fwd)
st <- c(mean(mm$vix[ok]), mean(mm$rv_fwd[ok]), cor(mm$vix[ok], mm$rv_fwd[ok]),
        cor(mm$rm[ok], mm$rv_fwd[ok]), mean(mm$vix[ok] > mm$rv_fwd[ok]))
long <- rbind(data.frame(date = mm$date, v = mm$vix, what = "VIX (implied, next 30 days)"),
              data.frame(date = mm$date, v = mm$rv_fwd, what = "realized vol, next 21 trading days"))
ggplot(long, aes(date, v, colour = what)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#8ba3c7", "#8b2635"), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 90)) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Annualised vol (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
The VIX is the volatility priced into one-month S&P 500 options, a risk-neutral expectation: forward-looking, but not a forecast under the real-world measure. It averages `r sprintf("%.1f", st[1])`% against `r sprintf("%.1f", st[2])`% realized, and exceeds realized vol on `r round(100 * st[5])`% of days: investors pay a **variance risk premium**. Its correlation with future realized vol is `r sprintf("%.2f", st[3])`, against `r sprintf("%.2f", st[4])` for the backward-looking RiskMetrics.
:::

## 📝 Quiz #1: RiskMetrics {.quiz-question}

RiskMetrics with $\lambda = 0.94$ is a GARCH(1,1) with

- [$\omega = 0$, $\alpha = 0.06$, $\beta = 0.94$]{.correct data-explanation="✅ σ²(t+1|t) = (1 − λ) r²(t) + λ σ²(t|t−1): no constant, weight 1 − λ = 0.06 on news and λ = 0.94 on the previous variance. α + β = 1, an IGARCH."}
- $\omega = 0$, $\alpha = 0.94$, $\beta = 0.06$
- $\omega = 0.06$, $\alpha = 0.94$, $\beta = 0$
- $\omega > 0$ estimated from the data, $\alpha + \beta = 0.94$

---

## 📝 Quiz #2: Realized Volatility {.quiz-question}

Why do practitioners compute $RV_t$ from 5-minute returns rather than from every tick?

- [Microstructure noise inflates RV at very high frequencies]{.correct data-explanation="✅ RV converges to integrated volatility as m grows only for the efficient price. Bid–ask bounce and discrete ticks add noise to every intraday return, and its contribution to RV grows with m."}
- Because $RV_t$ diverges as $m \to \infty$ even without noise
- Because the drift term dominates at high frequency
- Because tick data are not observable

---

## 📝 Quiz #3: Backtesting {.quiz-question}

A 95% VaR is exceeded on 0 of 500 days. Kupiec's test:

- [Rejects: 0 hits is far fewer than the 25 expected, so the VaR is too conservative]{.correct data-explanation="✅ With x = 0, LR = −2·500·ln 0.95 = 51.3 > 3.84. Kupiec's test is two-sided: too few hits means the bank holds a VaR far beyond the 5% quantile."}
- Does not reject: no hits is the best possible outcome
- Cannot be computed, because $\log \hat\pi$ is undefined
- Rejects only if the hits are clustered

---

## 📋 Key Formulas

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
| | |
|---|---|
| RiskMetrics | $\sigma^2_{t+1\mid t} = 0.06\,r_t^2 + 0.94\,\sigma^2_{t\mid t-1}$, an IGARCH |
| Realized volatility | $RV_t = \sum_{i=1}^m r_{t,i}^2 \to IV_t = \int_0^1\sigma^2_{t+s}\,ds$ |
| MEM / ACD(1,1) | $x_t = \psi_t\varepsilon_t$, $E\varepsilon_t = 1$; $\ \psi_t = \omega + \alpha d_{t-1} + \beta\psi_{t-1}$ |
| Autologit(1,1) | $P_t = 1/(1+e^{-w_t})$, $\ w_t = \varphi + \alpha\mathbb 1\{r_{t-1}>0\} + \gamma r_{t-1} + \beta w_{t-1}$ |
| VaR, indirect | $\widehat{\mathrm{VaR}}_t = \hat\mu_t + \hat\sigma_t q_p(\hat f_{\mathcal D})$ |
| CAViaR | $q_t^p = \omega + \beta q_{t-1}^p + \alpha|r_{t-1}|$, $\ \min\sum_t\rho_p(r_t - q_t^p)$ |
| Kupiec | $LR_{uc} = -2\log[(1-p)^{n-x}p^x] + 2\log[(1-\hat\pi)^{n-x}\hat\pi^x] \to \chi^2_1$ |

: {tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}
:::

---

## 📋 Summary

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
- $|r_t|$, $r_t^2$ and RiskMetrics are observable and model-free; GARCH $\hat\sigma_t^2$ is model-based
- RiskMetrics is an IGARCH with $\omega = 0$, $\alpha = 0.06$, $\beta = 0.94$
- Realized volatility converges to integrated volatility; noise sets the sampling interval at 5–15 minutes
- MEM and ACD model positive series as a conditional mean times a unit-mean shock
- Direction (autologit) and quantiles (VaR, CAViaR) are dynamic models in their own right
- On the S&P 500 the 99% normal VaR fails Kupiec's test; the tail, not the volatility, is the problem
:::
